items.title: We should be more ambitious with the software we build
items.content:
Since early this year, Michael Malis (of pgrust ) has been showing me interesting things he's done and saying

[W]e should be more ambitious 1 with the software we build

There is, understandably, a lot of skepticism about projects like pgrust because there are so many low-quality AI-generated projects out there. If I didn't know Malis and didn't look into it, I would just assume that pgrust was another vibe slopped project that's never going to work. But I know Malis well enough to trust his work without looking into it, and if you look into it a bit, you'll see that in testing pgrust, he's testing thoroughly enough that he's even uncovering real bugs in Postgres, such as this numerical bug that can cause valid SP-GiST operations to fail , this format cache bug that can cause incorrect results from JSONPath , this pgcrypto bug that can cause later operations to fail , multiple memory safety bugs in the dictionary loader 2 , this money overflow bug , etc.

This isn't to say that pgrust is bug free 3 , but it does indicate that there's a substantial amount of testing happening and, even if pgrust itself is never successful, just making the attempt will have improved Postgres in a durable way. The main pitch for pgrust is actually performance, and that's where the really interesting work is happening; if pgrust fails, it's possible that some of the optimizations they've demonstrated will make it into Postgres, Clickhouse, etc., but that's obviously less direct than filing Postgres bugs which get fixed.

That being said, I find it understandable that, every time I see pgrust discussed on a news aggregator, most people dismiss it as vibeslop garbage because almost all of these rewrite projects are slop. If I didn't know Malis, I would make the same assumption, because who has the time to look into all of these projects? Because I know Malis, I didn't bother to look at it; I just trusted him (I only found the above because I wanted to check on pgrust before using it as an example for this post).

As a consumer of software, everywhere you look, there's slow software that the creator is claiming is fast because the creator is touting some slop benchmark, e.g., here's one of multiple examples I saw yesterday , and of course low-quality software that doesn't work is more common than ever.

But, as a builder of software, it doesn't matter that almost all of these projects are vibeslop, that other people are out there shoveling out huge piles of crap and calling it gold. You can build things like pgrust or other projects that would've been too large to really be feasible in the past and, if you do a reasonable job with testing and benchmarking, that stuff can actually be good-enough quality to use.

If I were writing it, I would say "we can be more ambitious with the software we build" and not "we should", but Malis has been casually chatting with me when he's said this, so maybe he would say the same in an actual post; don't read too much into should vs. can here. What's interesting to me is how capabilities have advanced such that we can do a lot more.

Just for example, after hearing that OpenAI was going to use Cerebras for their SOTA models and not just fast-but-low-quality models like 5.3-Codex-Spark, I looked at where time on my computer would go if I was using a SOTA model, but 10x to 100x faster; some things that were already sometimes a bottleneck that would only get worse with a faster model were:

At the level of a "works for me" project, these are all things that can seriously be improved. I don't have much spare time at the moment but, even so, I built this regex engine that can be tweaked to be faster than other general-purpose regex libraries on any particular workload I care about , this ripgrep fork that uses the native code compiler from the regex engine and is faster for my codex ripgrep workloads (of course a text index is the better solution, but I've already worked on text indexing and this was a "just for fun"…

items.summary_ko: 글쓴이는 pgrust 프로젝트를 만든 Michael Malis의 작업을 근거로, 소프트웨어에 더 큰 야심을 가져야 한다고 주장한다. AI로 만든 저품질 프로젝트가 많아 pgrust에도 회의적인 시선이 있지만, Malis는 pgrust를 테스트하는 과정에서 Postgres의 실제 버그들을 여럿 찾아냈다. pgrust가 완벽하지는 않더라도, 시도 자체가 Postgres를 개선하는 데 기여했다고 평가한다.
items.content_ko: 글쓴이는 올해 초부터 Michael Malis가 보여준 여러 작업물을 보며, 소프트웨어는 더 야심 있게 만들어야 한다고 말해 왔다. pgrust 같은 프로젝트에는 저품질 AI 생성 프로젝트가 많다는 이유로 회의적인 시선이 있다. 하지만 글쓴이는 Malis를 신뢰하며, 직접 살펴보면 그가 pgrust를 충분히 철저하게 테스트하고 있다고 말한다. 그 과정에서 Postgres의 실제 버그가 여럿 드러났다. 예를 들어 유효한 SP-GiST 연산이 실패하게 만드는 수치 버그, JSONPath에서 잘못된 결과를 내게 하는 format cache 버그, 이후 연산을 실패하게 만드는 pgcrypto 버그, 사전 로더의 여러 메모리 안전성 버그, 금액 오버플로 버그 등이다. 글쓴이는 pgrust가 버그가 없다는 뜻은 아니라고 덧붙인다. 하지만 상당한 양의 테스트가 이루어지고 있으며, pgrust가 끝내 성공하지 못하더라도 이런 시도 자체가 Postgres를 여러 면에서 개선했다고 주장한다.

items.title: POSIX wordexp(3) is dangerous
items.summary: c, security
items.content:
wordexp(3) is a POSIX API for performing shell-style expansions from C.

It's often cited/recommended as a way to do tilde expansion (e.g. ~/foo to /home/me/foo ):

However, wordexp(3) is also dangerous! That last 0 argument is for the flags parameter.

By default, all expansion features are enabled, including command expansion :

Disabling this requires passing WRDE_NOCMD as a flag. Unfortunately, this

palliative at best in some libc implementations:

musl implements wordexp(3) by delegating to the system shell. It adds some

perfunctory scanning for command substitutions before delegating, but

fails to match some patterns that the underlying shell (like GNU Bash) can treat

macOS's libc implements wordexp(3) in a similar manner, delegating to

/usr/lib/system/wordexp-helper 1 . According to Julian Squires

this had the same bypass as musl as recently as 2023 , although I didn't bother

testing whether it's still effective now that the default macOS shell is zsh

Bottom line: don't use wordexp(3) on untrusted inputs, even with WRDE_NOCMD .

Previously, macOS's wordexp(3) would shell out to Perl. wordexp-helper appears to be the "modern" solution. ↩
items.title_ko: POSIX wordexp(3)은 위험하다
items.summary_ko: wordexp(3)은 쉘 방식의 확장을 C에서 수행하는 POSIX API로, 틸드 확장 용도로 자주 추천된다. 그러나 기본적으로 명령 치환까지 활성화되어 있어 신뢰할 수 없는 입력에 쓰면 위험하다. WRDE_NOCMD 플래그도 musl과 macOS libc 등 일부 구현에서는 충분한 방어가 되지 않는다.
items.content_ko: wordexp(3)은 C에서 쉘 스타일 확장을 수행하는 POSIX API이며, `~/foo`를 `/home/me/foo`로 바꾸는 틸드 확장 용도로 자주 권장된다. 하지만 기본 설정에서는 명령 치환을 포함한 모든 확장 기능이 켜져 있어 위험하다. 이를 막으려면 WRDE_NOCMD 플래그를 넘겨야 한다. 그러나 musl은 wordexp를 시스템 쉘에 위임하면서 명령 치환을 일부만 검사하기 때문에, GNU Bash가 처리할 수 있는 일부 패턴을 놓친다. macOS libc도 `/usr/lib/system/wordexp-helper`에 위임하는 방식이며, 작성자는 Julian Squires의 설명을 인용해 2023년까지 musl과 같은 우회 방법이 통했다고 전했다. 작성자의 결론은 WRDE_NOCMD를 쓰더라도 신뢰할 수 없는 입력에는 wordexp(3)을 사용하지 말라는 것이다.

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

items.title: A 10-year-old CNN outperforms frontier LLMs for skin cancer diagnosis
items.content:
Figure 1. Invasive melanoma on the ear, under 0.8 mm thick. Both LLMs called it a seborrhoeic keratosis and said it could be discharged. The CNN called it a melanoma. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC.

I showed these two images - a clinical photograph and a dermoscopic (skin microscope) image - to GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1, two of the most capable AI models available in October 2026. Both said it was a seborrhoeic keratosis, a harmless warty growth, and that the patient could be discharged. I then showed them to fine-tuned version of Inception v3, a convolutional neural network (CNN) first published by Google in 2015 and fine-tuned here on public dermatology images. The CNN got the right answer based on the dermoscopy view.

It was one of 200 biopsy-proven lesions I gave to all three. The CNN named the right diagnosis (out of 6 possiblities) for 125 of them (62%). The two frontier LLMs named it for 84 and 85 (42%). A ten-year-old network, fine-tuned for about twenty minutes, beat both of them at recognising skin cancer.

The lesions come from MILK10k , a public dataset released through the International Skin Imaging Collaboration in 2025, in which each lesion is photographed twice: a clinical close-up and a dermoscopic image taken through the illuminated magnifying lens dermatologists use. I drew 200 lesions at random, all confirmed by histopathology:

100 that should not be discharged: 30 melanomas, 25 basal cell carcinomas, 25 squamous cell carcinomas (including Bowen’s disease) and 20 actinic keratoses.

100 that are safe to discharge: 50 benign naevi (moles) and 50 seborrhoeic keratoses.

Every lesion was biopsied, including the benign ones, so these are harder to diagnose: a mole that somebody decided to cut out is one that worried a clinician.

Basal cell carcinoma on the trunk of a 75-year-old man. All three models answered correctly.

Invasive melanoma under 0.8 mm thick, with very little pigment. GPT-6 Astra called it a basal cell carcinoma with 95% confidence. Claude Fable 5.1 and the CNN called it a melanoma.

Seborrhoeic keratosis on the leg. Both LLMs called it an actinic keratosis and the CNN a squamous cell carcinoma: all three were wrong, though all three would have kept it rather than discharge it.

Figure 2. Three more of the 200 test lesions. Clinical photograph on the left, dermoscopic image on the right. Images: MILK10k , MILK study team, CC BY-NC.

The LLMs were given both images and nothing else, and asked, as a clinician might use them, for the most likely of the six diagnoses (or “unsure”), a confidence, a second choice, and whether the lesion could be safely discharged with no treatment, biopsy or follow-up. Both models got the same prompt at default settings, and neither refused a case.

The CNN is deliberately not state of the art. I used Inception v3 pretrained on everyday photographs and then fine-tuned all layers on 68,011 dermoscopic and clinical images from the ISIC Archive on a single H100 GPU. These 200 test lesions, and every other photograph of the same lesion or patient, were removed from its data (including the validation set) before training, so it had never seen them, and they were not used to choose the model or set its threshold. It scored both images of each lesion, combined them with most of the weight on the dermoscopic image, and chose from the same six diagnoses.

You can try the CNN yourself . Remarkably the model is small enough to run entirely in a phone browser using WebGPU. Nothing is uploaded, and its random sample button draws from these same 200 lesions.

items.title: Simple NetBSD webserver
items.summary: netbsd
items.content:
There might be time you want to have a sensible space in that untangible mess that is modern World Wide Web. The choices run slim and at some point there are ~three operating systems that you can trust having on your server 1 .

I’ll describe here the quick and proven route for running a NetBSD 11 web server - the ‘stock’ way with bozohttpd that requires only one additional package for HTTPS 2 . It probably won’t do if you expect heavy traffic, but for homebrew projects and small scale communities it should do just fine.

A VPS (or local machine or virtual machine) and a terminal emulator.

Maybe web-browser to check the results (though curl is quite sufficient for that imo).

I’m not affiliated but as far as recommendations go - I’m using netcup service, it looks okay. Not expensive and they already have NetBSD11 amd64 iso preloaded in their OS library to install OS on your machine.

There are others people recommend for netbsd:

If you can recommend or suggest even more - please email me, I’ll add it to the list list.

NetBSD has a small web-server that is sufficient for tons of stuff right out of the box - bozohttpd(8) . It is somewhat limited by design, but the manpage is quite useful and describes a lot of interesting stuff you can do with just marker files and simple command line options.

Some guides out there explain a path to run it using inetd(8) , it is kinda native internet “super-server” for unix but I didn’t like that it launches an instance of httpd (alias/hardlink to bozohttpd) on every connection. Bozohttpd is capable running as daemon itself, I like that option.

The only config httpd needs lies in command line options, which can be nicely wrapped in /etc/rc.conf with self-explanatory keys like this:

If you have something in /var/www/my_magical_domain/index.html, then after simple /etc/rc.d/httpd start voila - you already have it served via plain http. Simple as that.

I won’t explain usage of self-signed procedure, instead resorting to one of the most popular freeware certificate issuer on the internet - letsencrypt.

There are several methods of obtaining the certificates from them, I’m using acme-client package (installed via pkgin ) - it is a portable version of an openbsd tool, I’m most used to it.

We need couple more directories to expose our challenge and to keep the certificates on. Try to not use “4” as a private key - it’s been exposed recently, stick with prime numbers at least :)

mkdir -p /var/www/my_magical_domain/.well-known/acme-challenge

And we need a config file for our domain - /usr/pkg/etc/acme-client.conf :

api url "https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory"

account key "/usr/pkg/etc/acme/letsencrypt-privkey.pem"

alternative names { www.my_magical_domain }

domain key "/etc/ssl/private/my_magical_domain.key"

domain full chain certificate "/etc/ssl/my_magical_domain.fullchain.pem"

challengedir "/var/www/my_magical_domain/.well-known/acme-challenge"

Running acme-client my_magical_domain should do the trick and put the neccessary certs to their corresponding paths. Do not forget to wait for at least few hours after putting your vps IP address into domain A record - it has to be propagated everywhere properly and resolve for letsencrypt as well.

Afterwards we have to pass the keys to the bozohttpd, and that enables it serving the port 443 automatically. So an addition to /etc/rc.conf should look like this:

httpd_flags="-Z /etc/ssl/my_magical_domain.fullchain.pem /etc/ssl/private/my_magical_domain.key"

Restart httpd and Bob’s your uncle - we have a working web server showing whatever static files you put into the directory.

Now there is one more thing to that - Letsencrypt certificates expire after certain amount of time, so we have to renew them using same acme-client(1) program. The simplest way to do so would be a cronjob - daily or even weekly - that tries to update the certificate and then restarts the httpd, via crontab(5) :

0 2 * * 1 /usr/pkg/bin/acme-client…

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. We cannot yet be certain when the agent understood it was taking real world action, or to what extent it believed it was in a fictional test scenario; our analysis so far presents a…

items.content:
온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

마치 테러리스트가 인질극 벌이는데 인질 죽는다고 테러리스트 진압 안하겠다는 것과 같은 말이다.

총수, 의장 검찰 총원해서 조져 놓다가 사면을 해놓으니까 버릇이 안좋아 진건지 아니면 반도체좀 했다고 뭐가 된양인지 모르겠다만

앞으로 대한민국에서도 여당과 야당 합작으로 대기업 총수, 의장 사법처리하고 사면하지않고 만기 출소하는 케이스가 단 한 번이라도 나와서 명확하게 그 선례를 남겨놔야한다는게 내 생

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Dolly Parton's Imagination Library
items.content:
Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library is dedicated to inspiring a love of reading by gifting books free of charge to children from birth to age five, through funding shared by Dolly Parton and local community partners in the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia and Republic of Ireland.

Inspired by her father’s inability to read and write Dolly started her  Imagination Library in 1995 for the children within her home county. Today, her program spans five countries and gifts millions of free books each month to children around the world.

“When I was growing up in the hills of East Tennessee, I knew my dreams would come true. I know there are children in your community with their own dreams. They dream of becoming a doctor or an inventor or a minister. Who knows, maybe there is a little girl whose dream is to be a writer and singer.

The seeds of these dreams are often found in books and the seeds you help plant in your community can grow across the world.”

In 1995, Dolly Parton launched an exciting new effort,  Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library , to benefit the children of her home county in East Tennessee, USA. Dolly’s vision was to foster a love of reading among her county’s preschool children and their families by providing them with the gift of a specially selected book each month.

By mailing high quality, age-appropriate books directly to their homes, she wanted children to be excited about books and to feel the magic that books can create. Moreover, she could ensure that every child would have books, regardless of their family’s income

There is simply no limit on how far we can take this program and to what ends of the earth, but it is an absolute impossibility without your help. If your community or a community that you are aware of doesn’t yet offer this proven early childhood literacy program, then we challenge you to Get Involved! It’s actually quite easy to bring the Imagination Library to life in your community and we have an onslaught of available resources to help you Start A Program including a personal trainer which we like to call “Regional and State Directors” So come on, you can do it, follow this link to get a simple checklist of what you need to do to Get Onboard Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library.

items.title: The Slurptop: A home-built luggable that runs on power tool batteries
items.summary: art, hardware
items.content:
Table of Contents The Design Process | Power Delivery | Bill of Materials | Closing Thoughts

Prior to completing this project I didn't have a modern laptop. I also had never tried out a trackball mouse. After completing a Writerdeck and a Cyberdeck based on Raspberry Pi SBCs, I felt that it would be incredibly useful to have a full-fledged x86 portable computer. You know, a laptop. Why not spend two months designing, building, and refining a laptop myself instead of just hitting up Best Buy for a new laptop that's ready to go? I mean, I don't have good justification beyond "because I can, and I want to", but sometimes that's all the justification you need!

At the outset of the design process I started looking at Intel N50 and N100 mITX motherboards and PicoPSU power delivery, but started getting discouraged at the price prospect of something that was more expensive than a Raspberry Pi, consumed more power, didn't offer much more computing power than a Pi, and consumed significantly more power. That's when I figured if I was heading in a high power draw x86 setup, why not start shopping out some mini PCs?

That's where I found some decently spec'd out units with laptop processors and integrated graphics. These, I figured, would fit the bill for a machine that would be destined for some coding and light design work. Next up would be figuring out the power delivery.

Since my last folding screen Cyberdeck, I've been really enjoying designing within the Cyberpunk aesthetic. One of the aesthetic aspects that I felt the last build was missing was improvised part selection. Then I had the thought of powering the unit with a 24v power tool battery. The design aesthetic and the improvised hardware selection dovetailed beautifully in the design of the power delivery. The mini PC I bought had a 19v/5a power supply, and my power tool batteries were 24v. With a properly spec'd boost/buck converter, that should work perfectly both on the aesthetic requirement as well as the power and current requirement.

Now we get to the fun stuff: sketching out the design.

If you're interested in Cyberdecks, I'm sure you've seen a plethora of devices. From slabs without a hinging screen, to vintage computer style raising screens (like I used on my gray Cyberdeck), to absolutely awesome sliding designs like u/Personalitysphere's sliding modular Cyberdeck. I wanted something that would have the rough form factor of a laptop.

With the form factor decided on, the next step in every project I do is to gather up all the components, grab my calipers, and get to measuring and modeling in Blender. I make "good enough" 3d models of EVERYTHING. It's tedious and time consuming, but I wouldn't do it any other way. You can package everything so much nicer when using this method, and you run into WAY fewer problems during the assembly stage, WAY fewer redesigns and reprints, etc. This is the "measure twice" process when building a device like this, even though it's more along the lines of "measuer ten thousand times". Very worth it, and I highly recommend approaching things from this direction. Not to mention you're honing your ability to measure and model things, which is invaluable as a desinger.

After establishing the layout of the individual components, I start going through a process of sketching out designs and layouts. Usually I have a pretty clear vision of what I'm going for at this point, but a lot of design elements are "discovered" at this stage. It's also where some hard choices have to be made because establishing certain design elements sets you down a road where if you choose to go a different direction you can't just CTRL+Z you're way out of. You have to delete a LOT of work sometimes.

items.title: Broccoli2Shell: the Brotli decoder bug (CVE-2026-111497) - Affecting Node.js, Python, C library
items.content:
Brotli decoder 1.0.3 through 1.2.0. An out-of-bounds write that can lead to a crash, a memory leak or remote code execution. Rated 9.2 Critical (CVSS 4.0) by GitHub, High by Node.js.

Installing the update isn't enough. A running process keeps the old decoder until it restarts, and a container keeps it until you rebuild the image on a patched base and redeploy.

You're at risk if your code, or any library it uses, decompresses Brotli data that someone else controls. That happens in more places than you'd think, because HTTP clients decompress Brotli responses on their own.

Node's built-in fetch() decodes Content-Encoding: br responses automatically. So do Python's requests / urllib3 and aiohttp whenever a Brotli package is installed. Any server you talk to can send the payload, whether through webhooks, link previews, crawlers or "import from URL" features.

Express 5.0.0–5.3.0 and body-parser 2.0.0–2.3.0 inflate Brotli request bodies in parsers such as raw() and json() . Python frameworks and middleware that decode br bodies are exposed in the same way. A bare node:http server doesn't decode bodies by itself.

This means zlib.brotliDecompress*() , createBrotliDecompress() , brotli.decompress() , and any library that uses them on archives, caches or queue messages.

Express and body-parser don't contain the bug. They're just paths to it, so upgrading them won't help. Node.js bundles its own copy of Brotli, which means the system libbrotli doesn't matter there. Only the Node.js version does.

A Brotli stream is split into blocks, and the decoder switches between block types as it reads them. Before the fix, DecodeBlockTypeAndLength() in c/dec/decode.c returned a plain boolean, so callers couldn't tell a malformed stream from one that just needed more input. On the fast path, the decoder ignored the return value altogether.

A crafted stream can request a block switch that can't happen. The decoder took that to mean "need more input" and kept adding attacker bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer, writing past its end. The overwrite corrupts nearby decoder state. That's how a malformed stream can turn into a memory leak or code execution.

The upstream fix is google/brotli commit 0ed4268 , along with 50a9b70 , b418fa8 and da98063 . It returns a hard format error, BROTLI_DECODER_ERROR_FORMAT_BLOCK_SWITCH (−17), to the caller. The bug is tracked as CWE-252 (unchecked return value) and CWE-787 (out-of-bounds write).

The PyPI packages Brotli and brotlicffi compile the same C decoder. Your code doesn't need to import them to be exposed. If either one is installed, these clients use it on their own:

Don't wait for your scanner. When this was disclosed, pip-audit, Dependabot and Safety didn't reliably flag the affected PyPI versions. The CVE record named the upstream Google repository, not the PyPI packages. GitHub's advisory now lists both packages (PYSEC-2026-4322 and PYSEC-2026-4323), but check by hand anyway.

If your bindings come from your Linux distribution (for example python3-brotli ) and not from PyPI, the fix arrives through your distribution's security updates.

The bug is in Google's reference C decoder, not in Node.js or Python. Anything that ships or links Brotli 1.0.3 through 1.2.0 may be affected, even before an advisory names it.

Decoders rewritten in other languages aren't a concern. The Java, JavaScript and C# ports, which pdf.js, iText and HtmlUnit use, can't reach the bug. The Go port (andybalholm/brotli) had the same logic error, but it would only have crashed, and it was fixed on 23 October. Rust's brotli-decompressor catches the condition and returns an error. Code execution is only possible in the C decoder.

Many projects ship a private copy of the C decoder instead of using your system's library. A distribution update doesn't fix those: each project has to update its copy. We searched GitHub for vendored copies and read their headers, and last rechecked them on 25 October 2026. A copy is patched if it…
items.title_ko: Broccoli2Shell: Brotli 디코더 버그(CVE-2026-111497), Node.js·Python·C 라이브러리 영향
items.summary_ko: Brotli 디코더 1.0.3~1.2.0의 범위 밖 쓰기 취약점으로, 충돌, 메모리 누출, 원격 코드 실행으로 이어질 수 있다. GitHub은 CVSS 4.0 기준 9.2(Critical), Node.js는 High로 평가했다. 업데이트 설치만으로는 부족하며, 실행 중인 프로세스와 컨테이너는 재시작 또는 패치된 이미지로 재빌드해야 적용된다.
items.content_ko: 외부가 제어하는 Brotli 데이터를 압축 해제하는 코드나 라이브러리가 있으면 위험에 노출된다. Node.js의 fetch()는 Content-Encoding: br 응답을 자동으로 디코딩하며, Python의 requests, urllib3, aiohttp도 Brotli 패키지가 설치되어 있으면 같은 방식으로 동작한다. Express 5.0.0~5.3.0과 body-parser 2.0.0~2.3.0은 raw()와 json() 등에서 Brotli 요청 본문을 해제한다. 순수 node:http 서버는 그 자체로 본문을 디코딩하지 않는다. 본문은 zlib.brotliDecompress*(), createBrotliDecompress() 등 관련 API 설명 부분에서 끊겨 있다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

items.title: I refuse to accept a censored Internet. Join Me at FOSDEM 27
items.content:
As one of the managers of the Digital Dissident Devroom , I invite you to be part of a conversation we cannot afford to ignore.

Around the world, people are being silenced, monitored, and denied access to information. Free software can help change that, but only if we build it together. We need tools people can trust and control to communicate safely, expose the truth, and resist censorship.

This devroom brings together developers, researchers, activists, and everyone committed to digital freedom. We want real solutions, honest lessons, and collaboration across projects, not product pitches.

If you believe technology should serve people, not control them, join us. Bring your ideas, experience, and questions. Let’s build the tools that help keep freedom alive.

Our focus complements other devrooms, including Decentralized Internet and Privacy, which explores the broader decentralized ecosystem. While they focus on technologies, we focus on the people under threat and the complete chain of tools that can protect them.

Go to FOSDEM’s official CFP portal from here and login or register.

Then fill in the form and select “Digital Dissident” as a track.

Please note that by doing this you also accept the FOSDEM Code of Conduct.

Define: Digital Dissident Developer Room

Privacy and anonymity tools each have a home at FOSDEM: the network, security, decentralised and messaging rooms, and various main-track and lightning talks. Someone living under an authoritarian regime (Russia, Iran, China, Belarus, Myanmar and others) never uses a single tool, though. Their day-to-day security depends on a chain of tools that has to hold up end to end:

reaching the network at all (censorship circumvention),

collecting, verifying and storing evidence safely,

publishing or leaking it without exposing the author,

doing all this on devices and infrastructure that are themselves a risk.

The weakest link decides the outcome. Talks about one tool rarely cover how it fits with the others, where the seams are, or what breaks at the hand-offs (for example, a circumvention transport that is fingerprinted, or a messenger whose push notifications tie your identity to a Google or Apple account). Nobody currently owns that cross-project view.

What this devroom does. It brings developers of circumvention, anonymity, messaging, publishing and whistleblowing tools into one room. It is deliberately not about any single project. Each session is judged on how well it advances the toolchain: interoperability, shared threat models, shared failure data, and shared engineering practice.

Why now. Censorship in Russia, Iran and China has grown much more sophisticated. It now includes national allow-lists and whitelist-only internet shutdowns, TLS and QUIC fingerprinting, deep packet inspection with active probing, throttling of specific protocols, mobile internet shutdowns, app-store removal of circumvention tools, and mandatory state-run messengers and “sovereign internet” routing. Anti-censorship developers have responded with pluggable transports, domain fronting alternatives, mixnets, decentralised and email-based messaging, and new obfuscation protocols. Progress is fast but fragmented. At FOSDEM 2026 the relevant talks were scattered: Vitaly Repin’s “The Russian Censorship Circumvention, Tom’s Traps, and Jerry’s VPN: A 5-Year Journey” (Saturday, H.1302, Network track) drew a large audience, while NymVPN and Delta Chat’s multi-relay messaging (both Sunday, Decentralized Internet and Privacy devroom) and other related talks ran in other rooms. A single devroom lets that audience and those speakers meet in one place.

Relationship to the existing “Decentralized Internet and Privacy” devroom. That room covers decentralised technology broadly (P2P protocols, browsers, code collaboration, key infrastructure), and censorship or anonymity is only a part of it. Digital Dissident is different: the organising principle is a user under threat and the end-to-end chain…

items.title: Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs
items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

items.title: Growing Majority of Americans Convinced That AI Is Bad for Society: Public opinion is not on the AI industry's side.
items.content:
In case there was any doubt over the powerful tide of anti-AI sentiment, a new poll shows that most Americans are incredibly pessimistic about the technology.

The poll , conducted in a collaboration between the Washington Post, ABC News , and the research and consulting firm IPSOS, showed that 57 percent of Americans now believe AI is outright bad for society, while just 42 percent say it’s good.

And the ardent pessimists dwarf the bullish optimists. A full 17 percent think AI is in fact “extremely” bad, compared to a measly 2 percent who say it’s extremely good.

The poll, which gathered responses from over 2,500 adults, comes after months of remarkably alarmist rhetoric from the AI industry, even compared to its history of casually doomsaying about its own tech.

AI companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, have each revealed incidents in which their agentic models went on rogue hacking sprees that targeted other companies and even government websites . Insiders, meanwhile, have made sensational claims about the existential danger posed by AI — and the reckless, and perhaps cultish, naïveté of the people building it.

These fears were met with calls to slow down AI development. Industry leaders haven’t agreed to such a slowdown , but they made a show of signing a non-binding agreement to regulate themselves after meeting with president Donald Trump last month.

Significant anti-AI sentiment, it’s worth noting, goes back years. But the latest revelations over the tech’s threat to cybersecurity and critical infrastructure have added more urgency and teeth to these concerns. An overwhelming 73 percent of Americans say there’s a high or very high risk of AI hacking secure computer systems, the poll found. A longstanding fear such as AI eliminating many jobs , meanwhile, has 65 percent of Americans viewing it as a high or very high risk.

A majority may view AI as a net negative, but there’re still sizable splits in opinion by demographic. Some 65 percent of Americans under 30 say AI is bad for society, for instance, while only 53 percent of Americans over 40 hold the same view.

Across political lines, 63 percent of Democrats and 58 percent of independents are in the negative societal impact camp, but only 51 percent of Republicans view AI this way.

On the flip side, Americans are feeling less convinced by the purported upsides of AI, with only 34 percent thinking there’s a big chance that it will make everyday tasks easier, and a paltry 13 percent believing it will create many new jobs.

One of the most vigorous outlets of AI pushback as been opposition to data centers , which the poll shows no signs of slowing down. A sweeping 66 percent of Americans oppose new data center construction in the US, with the share at an overwhelming 76 percent among Democrats and 50 percent among Republicans. The figures are higher when the threat is closer to home: 81 percent of Democrats and 58 percent of Republicans oppose a new center being built in their own community.

items.title: The result of the C++26 DIS ballot
items.content:
C++26 failed its DIS ballot. As far as I know, it is the first C++ draft to fail one. Robert Seacord,

the convenor of the C committee, wrote that he doesn’t think any language standard from SC22 has ever

failed its ballot before, and Daveed Vandevoorde, a member of the WG21 Direction Group

( P5000R1 ), wrote that no earlier C++ draft got even a single vote

against. So reflection, std::execution , library hardening, and contracts are all in a draft that ISO hasn’t approved, and nobody knows yet

The ballot closed on 23 October 2026, and Robert Seacord, the convenor of the C committee,

I kept this series neutral while the vote was open and didn’t want to push anyone toward either

side. The vote is over, so I can say where I stand.

I love contracts as an idea, and I have missed them since they were removed from C++20. I have

always cared about API design, about libraries, good interfaces, and frameworks, and that is also

why I am in LEWG. My reasons for liking contracts come from that experience. Checking is one

benefit, and a good one: the program can verify its own assumptions. The second axis, which I

care about just as much, is documentation. A precondition or a postcondition in the signature records

the intent of the API designer, so users know what to expect and how to use the function, and a

documentation system such as Doxygen or cppreference.com can show it right there. A comment can say

the same thing, but nothing keeps it true. It can drift away from the code without anyone noticing.

A contract is part of the code. The compiler checks it together with the function, and when the

checks are enabled, a violation fails loudly, so this documentation can’t quietly go stale. Concepts

already give us both for the types a function accepts, at compile time. Contracts are the part that

is still missing, the one that does the same for the values at run time. I would love to see

contracts in the standard, and it is a pity they didn’t make it this time. My preference is to keep

them. If the design comes out better because of this, that is a good result too.

This isn’t an abstract question for me. I have started teaching C++26 contracts in my workshops, and

Part 2 explained the two conditions a DIS

has to meet. The draft missed both of them:

Votes in favor, from the voting (P-)members at least two-thirds 12 of 20, which is 60%

Negative votes, from all bodies that voted no more than 25% 9 of 22, which is 41%

Two-thirds of 20 needs 14 votes in favor, and the draft got 12. A quarter of 22 allows five negative

votes, and the draft got nine. Either one alone would have failed the draft.

The official result names every country. Nine voted No: Denmark, Finland, Iran, Italy, Japan,

Luxembourg, Romania, Spain, and Sweden. Each of them sent comments with its vote. France and Ireland

abstained but also sent comments, so 11 countries commented in total. Poland and the United States

abstained. I am a member of the Polish national body.

The comments themselves aren’t available yet. The ISO/IEC Directives (clause 2.6.5 of Part 1)

require a full report within 12 weeks of the vote’s end, including the result, the committee chair’s

decision, and the full text of the comments. For a ballot that closed on 23 October, this is

mid-January 2027 at the latest. At the committee-draft stage, WG21 published that kind of report as

N5028 . I don’t know if it will do the same this time.

Poland’s position on C++ is decided in a technical committee of the Polish Committee for

Standardization, KT 331. Its ballot asked whether Poland should reject the DIS and send technical

comments to ISO. The vote didn’t pass, so Poland told ISO “Abstention”, and no technical comments

I won’t share the tally or say who voted how. This is an internal vote, and I don’t know whether it

may be published. A few votes decide whether Poland says something or nothing at all.

items.title: OpenAI and Anthropic cut their LLM prices by up to 80% within a few months. Why?
items.content:
Let’s look at a quick timeline of the major LLM model announcements from both OpenAI and Anthropic over the past few months. All pricing numbers provided are input MTok / output MTok / cache read MTok .

OpenAI announced GPT-5.6 Sol and Luna. Sol is the direct successor to GPT 5.5 at the same price of $5 / $30 / $0.50 , while Luna is a small model specifically designed for cheaper use cases at $1 / $6 / $0.10 . They also announced a Terra model that’s in between those two models, but few cared about it.

Anthropic announced Claude Sonnet 5, which Anthropic claimed to be closer to their Opus models, but feedback was mixed. Notably, it had launch pricing of $2 / $10 / $0.20 which was initially supposed to be temporary but would go up.

Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5, which was a long-awaited major-version update given the impact Opus 4.5 had on the rise of agentic coding, at a price of $5 / $25 / $0.50 (similar to GPT-5.6 Sol). Although some of the provided benchmark results surprisingly exceeded those of the much larger Fable 5, real-world feedback was more mixed.

OpenAI announces that they cut the price of GPT-5.6 Luna by 80% (???) to $0.20 / $1.20 / $0.02 .

Model quality vs. Cost-per-task for GPT-5.6 Luna after the massive price reduction. Top-and-left is better, and if OpenAI didn’t do the 80% price cut, it would have lost to DeepSeek V4 Pro. via OpenAI

Anthropic announces the temporary Sonnet 5 price cut for the launch is now permanent.

OpenAI announces that they are cutting the price for GPT-5.6 Sol by ~20% ( $4 / $20 / $0.40 ) for the next three months.

Anthropic announced Fable 5.1 at a price of $10 / $50 / $0.25 , which, in addition to having strictly better benchmark performance in all areas than Fable 5 from June at $10 / $50 / $1 , cut the cache read cost by 75%.

When using agents for coding, cache read costs are the vast majority (96% - 99%) of the total token expenditure as the cache is what contains the entire previous conversation each turn. Additionally, the cache tends to be hit around 90 - 100% of the time (varies by the infrastructure of the LLM inference provider). Taken together, a 75% reduction in the cache read cost correlates to a 70-75% reduction in the cost of using the model—obviously notable, even if cache costs are typically a footnote!

OpenAI announced GPT-6 Astra, which is similar in size to Fable 5.1 and has similar pricing at $10 / $50 / $1 but without the lower cache read cost. Astra’s model performance is indeed comparable to Fable.

OpenAI announced GPT-6 Sol at at a shocking price of $2 / $10 / $0.20 that halves the input and output price relative to the temporarily-discounted GPT-5.6 Sol! They simultaneously released GPT-6 Luna also at half the input and output price ( $0.10 / $0.50 / $0.01 ) of the previous version.

On the same exact day , Anthropic announced Claude Opus 5.5, where it’s explicitly stated “Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that”. Its price of $4 / $20 / $0.20 is much lower in total than Opus 5’s due to a 20% input/output cost cut and a larger cache read cut, resulting in a total cost reduction of 40-60% for a model that’s even better than Fable 5.1 (I have quite a lot of things to say about Opus 5.5, but that’s for another post).

It turned out that GPT-6 Sol was a dud performancewise, so a week later OpenAI announced GPT-6.1 Sol, which surprisingly has comparable performance to Astra (can confirm after personal use), but OpenAI casually cut the cache price in half ( $2 / $10 / $0.10 ) matching Anthropic’s 5%-of-input cache read cost, making this model family cumulatively 75% cheaper.

Overall, starting from the release of the GPT-5.6 model families in June to now, the cost of using these popular LLMs has cratered, which is not something I would have expected a year ago. items.title: “AI Skills” are worthless in 2026
items.summary: ai-tooling, practices
items.content:
When I was first learning the C programming language, in my early 20s, it was common knowledge that of the two ways to increment a variable, i++ was slower than ++i . The post-increment function returned the original value of i , which meant stashing a copy of that value before performing the increment. Pre-increment avoided this wasteful operation.

And by “common knowledge” I really mean folklore, because I turned 20 in 1995 and even by then, the most basic of optimising compilers knew to check if you ever used the return value of i++ , and if not, skip the operation to save it.

Scratch an old programmer and you'll probably find a dozen or so ingrained habits that, in an era where CPUs are doing branch prediction and code reordering, are just as likely to make their program slower.

It makes sense to believe that all the tricks we come up with with to make models behave better, the ways of working with models that get us to a useful result faster, if they work, are going to be folded back into the product, packaged, and become the default experience a few months later. And yet, in five years, I’m sure there will be old heads doggedly adding “you are an experienced software developer, make no mistakes” to their custom instructions.

I'm not saying it's worthless to keep up with the state of the art. You still need to be able do your job today, to the best of your ability. But a skill that can be picked up in a few weeks, and will be obsolete in a few months, has no value outside the moment.

Eighteen months ago, I was sitting in a crowded room watching a CEO enthusiastically declare that it was time to get on the AI train, because if you didn't get on it right now you'd be left behind. Maybe I'm getting old, but in a world where Google, Facebook, the iPod, iPhone and iPad, and so many other examples have shown that getting it right is more valuable than getting in first, I feel content to just keep pace with the pack, ready to pull Steven Bradbury if and when the time comes.

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. items.title: On the line, online | Long-Haul Mag
items.content:
How Kickstarter Workers Organized a Fully Remote Strike

Just days before our strike was set to begin, the Contract Action Team had to move quickly to figure out a format to accommodate our fully remote shop. There was no technical need to assemble together in order to stop production, but we understood that a picket of some form would offer an essential element of collectivity or solidarity for our action. We didn’t have an office to picket in front of and our workers are across the country. We asked, how does a striking union picket over Zoom? A staffer sent us a sample picket line schedule for a nurses’ strike, and I adapted it as best I could for the bargaining unit. Our daily schedule for the 42 days of striking was as follows:

11am : Strike captains and the bargaining committee met to go over the plan for the day and process insights from the day prior.

12pm : All striking workers met on Zoom to play an ice breaker game, discuss updates, hold Q&As using a rapid polling tool, and discuss breakout room activities. Each member chose their preferred project to work on, such as proposal writing, Twitch streaming to aid our fundraising, and social media strategizing.

3pm: Activity breakout rooms closed and we opened our union Zoom up to the public. Striking workers gave speeches, and one or two guest speakers gave a talk.

4pm or later: Bargaining, if we could get management to the table that day.

A highlight among the breakout room projects was, broadly, “paperwork,” perhaps the least visible (and, honestly, the most tedious) aspect of our strike. But working through many pages of unemployment and later COBRA forms allowed us to solve a practical problem together and take care of each other in a way that bolstered our open-ended strike viability.

This format served our needs and kept us out on strike until we won, but there are a few changes I’d recommend for the next remote shop to go on strike.

One, I would have planned for a strike much earlier, perhaps before we even started bargaining. Much of the strike preparation was done just weeks or days before our strike, but we would have been much more prepared to answer our coworkers’ most pressing questions and lightened the load of strike leadership, especially just before and just after the strike started.

I’d also recommend a plan for combatting Zoom fatigue. Yes, workers in distributed shops are used to long days at a computer. But hours of collaborating synchronously during what for most of us was the most stressful event of our lives took its toll, especially in the first few weeks where there was no end to the work stoppage in sight. Weeks into our strike we eventually took “touch grass” days fully away from Zoom to volunteer in our respective communities. Next time I’d incorporate these offline days much earlier and perhaps even consider the idea of a more asynchronous strike. Do we need to be on Zoom together for 4+ hours every single day of a strike? Can we work on our strike projects on our own time instead of in a breakout room? Spending a few hours on Zoom every day in the early days was important to manage our collective fears and foster cohesion, but I don’t think the same daily format is necessary weeks or months into an open-ended strike.

In addition to what we’d change, it’s also worth reflecting on what went well with this hastily planned format. Finding a way to hold anonymous Q&As and host rapid polls was key to understanding the needs and desires of the unit. This allowed strike leadership to ensure all major (and many minor) decisions were made democratically.

As more and more distributed shops build toward work stoppages, we as organizers must continue to adapt existing strategies to best support our coworkers on the picket line. Solidifying our remote strike programming is crucial for sustaining an open-ended strike and increasing our leverage at the bargaining table.

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 다른 이용자에게 매니저의 책임과 권한이 위임될 수 있습니다.

매니저의 부재로 인해 운영에 지장이 있다고 판단될 경우, 다른 이용자가 권한을 위임받아 마이너 갤러리를 운영할 수 있습니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

items.title: Overgrown, when plants invade your abandoned tabs
items.content:
I was doing a little creative exercise the other day around the word "Overgrowth". The first thing that came to mind was an apocalyptic scene, something like The Walking Dead or The Last of Us, where plants tend to overgrow abandoned buildings.

I then wanted to apply this idea to the digital world, and the word "abandoned" made me think of my browser tabs... What if my tabs were slowly taken over by plants the longer I left them unread? What if I had to clear away these invasive plants to access my tabs again? A bit like trying to open a door that's been overgrown...

So I built this fun little Chrome extension that does just that. It won't necessarily make me read my tabs more but it's ok.

Originally, I was thinking about blocking users from closing their overgrown tabs until they slash all plants, but I thought it would be too annoying... 😅

The code is organised in 3 main parts: the background logic, the content script to display the plants and animation on the tabs and the popup folder that handles the UI of the extension itself.

The background.js file starts the jungle on each open tab and forgets it when it closes.

This folder handles the UI for the extension with some small components for the time setting, the weapon choice, the list of tabs and their current stat.

The content folder contains the SVGs for the plants and the weapons, the logic to position and grow the clusters, the neglect clock and the sounds.

I've been wanting to get back into building things for a while now and this project felt like a small, fun way to start. I'm writing this on a new computer so I currently "only" have 22 tabs open but 14 of them are already completely overgrown... 😂 It might not make me read them more but slashing through the vines makes coming back to them more fun! 🪚🌿

Still quite hairy, and not something I’d like to see in the wild, but nonetheless it’s understandable without knowing any precedence rules beyond arithmetic and comparison. Outside of this contrived example, though, the expressions that will now require parentheses are relatively rare (353 lines needed changes out of the million+ lines of code in the Zig codebase).

In practice, going forward, you will only need to remember the rules around operator combinations that still have a defined/unambiguous precedence. For example, when reading or writing code involving arithmetic operators, you’ll only need to remember the following precedence table:

You might notice that there isn’t anything too surprising there, and that lack of surprise was a (subjective) guiding principle for what should and should not require parentheses. As an example, while % has unambiguous precedence with regards to addition/subtraction operators, parentheses must be used when mixing % with multiplication/division operators, and with itself. However, this, and other ambiguous operator combinations, aren’t something you’ll need to commit to memory. Any (future) code you read will already have parentheses to disambiguate, and for any code you write, the compiler will let you know when you need parentheses.

For the full explanation, and to see the relevant precedence tables pertaining to other operators, see the updated Precedence section of the language reference .

My personal recommendation would be option 1, as the process of redetermining the intended evaluation order for these uncommon precedence scenarios can occasionally serve to uncover bugs ( here’s an example of that ).

If you go with option 2, I’d still recommend perusing the diff afterwards to ensure that nothing looks unusual, or is different than you expected/intended. A potentially common example of that is something like a orelse b() catch c which previously evaluated to (a orelse b()) catch c , but changing that to a orelse (b() catch c) likely makes more sense, even if the end result is unaffected. Also worth noting that in some scenarios, redundant parentheses will be added by zig fmt --upgrade (e.g. you might see something like a orelse ((b + c) - d) where the parentheses around b + c are unnecessary), so avoiding that will take a bit of manual cleanup.

That’s about it. I’m hopeful that this change will make bugs stemming from misremembered precedence rules much less likely, and that it will put some attention onto any of those bugs that may currently exist.

items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Big Tech is cashing in on AI while the rest of corporate America sees no financial returns — report outlines how rising token costs threaten to squeeze corporate profit margins.
items.content:
AI spending is generating revenue for technology providers, but most other S&P 500 companies have yet to show comparable gains in productivity or profit margins, a report by Apollo’s Daily Spark analysis has shown.

America’s AI chip rules keep changing — and the rest of the world is paying the price

Demand for data center CPUs has surged, and AI agents are responsible

Artificial intelligence has helped fuel a boom in technology spending, but the financial benefits remain difficult to spot across much of corporate America. Apollo Global Management chief economist Torsten Slok said on October 24 that revenue per worker and profit margins were rising for the Magnificent Seven technology stocks while remaining flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500.

Notably, Slok’s analysis found no clear evidence that AI is boosting productivity growth, despite heavy investment in the technology. Revenue per worker and profit margins have risen among the Magnificent Seven but remain flat across the other 493 companies in the S&P 500, according to the report. “Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok wrote.

Running AI models at scale can quickly drive up costs since many providers charge by token usage, so bills climb as employees make more requests or AI agents process data and handle increasingly complex tasks. Slok said mainstream companies were beginning to view token spending as a cost center rather than a source of growth. Venture capital-backed businesses are spending more on tokens, he noted, while established companies have less incentive to pay for the newest models if cheaper alternatives can do the job.

That creates a problem for AI providers hoping to turn growing adoption into a lasting revenue stream. Selling more computing power and model access can boost suppliers’ sales, but customers need to see corresponding gains in productivity, revenue or operating costs to keep spending at the same pace. Moreover, if AI expenses rise without a measurable improvement in business performance, the additional spending could weigh on margins.

“AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.” Slok added. “The bottom line is that the AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7, and so far, there is no evidence that revenue growth or margins are improving outside the tech sector.”

(Image credit: Apollo ) Slok’s analysis also points to a broader limitation: AI adoption remains concentrated among a relatively small group of companies. Unless usage spreads across more industries and produces measurable results, the technology’s effect on the wider economy could remain limited.

IBM CEO says open weight models are now irresistibly good and cheap on-prem

90 percent of the performance at ten percent of the price, in just two or three racks, is hard to beat

After threatening AI export bans, China allows DeepSeek to keep selling

OpenAI disables internet access during model training while Anthropic issues another mea culpa

IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has told investors that open weight models now make brilliant sense for on-prem enterprise use.

Speaking on the company’s Q3 earnings call, Krishna said that in 2024 closed frontier models were plainly superior to open alternatives.

“If you ran some assessment, some benchmark, and it was broad-based, not narrow, the top model might score a 70, and the open model might score a 20 or a 30.”

“In late 2025, we began to see that gap shrink, where maybe the gap was not 70 to 20 or 30, it was 70 to 50,” he continued.

The CEO said open weight models currently deliver “anywhere from 25 percent to 10 percent of the token cost of the frontier models. That is very attractive given that they’re now 90 percent as effective.”

“It’s a simple question for any enterprise. Would you like something that’s 10 percent of the cost if it’s 90 percent as good as the best, or do you want to pay that 10 times higher cost?”

Krishna thinks businesses will most often choose not to incur the higher costs.

“Then the question is: how many tasks require that? I would tell you some do, but the vast majority, summarizing an email, examining a contract, answering a customer call, composing an email, all of those can be done as well with the much cheaper answer.”

The CEO said those numbers mean IBM is seeing booming interest in on-prem AI infrastructure. While he thinks most businesses can build useful AI infrastructure in just two or three racks, he feels many will struggle to get it running.

“The question becomes: how do you do that?” he said. “The question that the enterprise struggles with is: ‘Where are my kernel engineers? Where are the people who worry about the underlying network? Who can make sure that the model is clustered on GPUs that are close to each other in network proximity? Who can make sure that you’re doing the right caching of results so you get an incredible response?’”

He didn’t have answers, other than to say IBM will produce software that eases AI deployments. Krishna also predicted demand for on-prem AI will spur sales of Big Blue’s Spyre mainframe accelerator cards.

The CEO said current-gen z17 mainframes have delivered $1bn more revenue than any previous model, and said Big Blue’s new rackable models delivered “the strongest midrange launch in IBM Z in nearly two decades.” Mainframe revenue, however, fell 20 percent – as IBM expects given it’s now 18 months since it launched the z17.

IBM’s infrastructure revenue grew five percent year-over-year to $3.7 billion, much slower improvement than recorded by rivals Dell, HPE, and Lenovo.

Software did rather better, scoring nine percent growth to reach $7.8 billion for the quarter. Red Hat was the star, growing eleven percent and increasing annual recurring revenue by 30 percent. Some of that future revenue is for Red Hat’s virtualization products, which have now won $800 million of deals, with a pipeline of a further $750 million. That’s a solid result for a product line launched in 2024, and IBM believes there’s more to come given the possibility some VMware users are on the move.

items.title: writing about pratt parsing so I remember it
items.summary: c, plt
items.content:
I got bored and wanted to make a parser of C expressions. this will probably become a compiler at some point. previously, I’ve made a calculator using shunting yard , but with an itch to perhaps make a compiler of some kind, I looked at pratt parsing .

you won’t find much information about pratt parsing in a conventional learning path of computer science. the dragon book , for all it talks about parsing, doesn’t mention it. as far as I’m aware, most programming language courses will probably teach either LR or recursive descent depending on how academic it is. pratt parsing specifically appears to be relegated mostly to compiler development and PLT circles. the most mainstream mention I know of it is in crafting interpreters ; wikipedia also links a few other posts. I used the crafting interpreters text to get my bearings, but I also wanted to practice reading formal papers more, so I tried using Pratt’s original paper text as much as possible. it did take a bit more time than I’d have liked to wrap my mind around how the recursion fits into the operator precedence, but it did just click all at once, namely once I related it back to shunting yard. so now I’m writing the observations down so I don’t forget. maybe it’s useful to you.

the shunting yard algorithm is, comparatively, much simpler than pratt. you have an output stream and an operator stack. operators are defined with their binding powers, where higher binding power means it binds tighter to its arguments (e.g. * has higher binding power in arithmetic than + ). in the simplest description of shunting yard, for every token in the input stream:

a very primitive shunting yard in C, where expressions are converted to postfix notation, could be:

the problem with shunting yard is that it’s not very extensible to new behavior . for example, the algorithm has no concept of “subexpressions” in the recursive sense; adding parentheses means attaching special functionality to the ) token for popping off the stack until reaching the matching ( . that’s not hard in its own right, but more complex behavior like unary operators, right-associative expressions, functions with variable arguments, etc. will get messy . this is where the transformation to pratt parsing comes in.

the core realization to turn shunting yard into pratt is, instead of using an explicit stack for operator precedence, using the call stack to implicitly be inside of subexpressions as we need them. unlike recursive descent, you don’t nest calls through every level of precedence for every expression, but rather only nest and return when entering subexpressions.

unfortunately, there’s no clean “intermediate” step for this. you kind of just have to thrust it all through the wringer and look at the output. here’s the simplest pratt-style parser I can show in c, equivalent to the shunting yard parser before:

on its own, this doesn’t look too exciting. I made the stack implicit. big whuff. but! there are two neat things here:

these combined allow for simple & straightforward extensibility. here’s all it takes to add parentheses into the mix:

want to add even more operators? coalesce the get_bindpower() function with choosing the subroutine to run, storing “rules” as a struct of the binding power, prefix subroutine, and postfix subroutine. the core stays simple while all the operators run in their own little functions! I’m not going to paste another blob of code here, but that setup is described in the crafting interpreters chapter . it’s so elegant!

hope this helps anyone else. happy parsing :)
